structure.title: IV. Results (A-D: infrastructure, benefit programs, workfare, heterogeneity)

observations.statement: The estimand is the sharp RD coefficient on crossing the village population cutoff (one thousand residents) in equation (1), interpreted as the effect of allocation into a smaller gram panchayat.

Two identifying assumptions are stated explicitly: no manipulation of the running variable around the cutoff, and continuity of village covariates at the threshold; manipulation is argued implausible since the delimitation rule was unforeseeable at census time.
observations.quote: the delimitation process was not foreseeable at the time of the preceding census

observations.statement: Authors choose to estimate the sharp discontinuity rather than a fuzzy RD instrumenting for one component of the treatment bundle, since crossing the cutoff changes GP population, compactness and homogeneity simultaneously.

A second design, labeled the alternative RD, is introduced using the population of other villages in the same pre-delimitation GP as the running variable, serving as both an additional estimate and an identification check.

Authors enumerate several empirical checks (other-state comparison, noncompliant UP districts, a placebo using the earlier census, split-ineligible villages) intended to rule out that another program uses the same population threshold.

Analysis combines Census of India rounds, the SHRUG village linkage panel, the Socioeconomic and Caste Census, Mission Antyodaya, the NREGS Public Data Portal, GP financial accounts, and state election commission records.
The unit of observation is the census village, stated to be advantageous because villages nest within GPs so outcomes are measured consistently regardless of GP assignment.

Two delimitation episodes anchor the sample periods: the 1995 delimitation using 1991 census population, and the 2015 delimitation using 2011 census population, with outcomes spanning 2001 to 2019-2020.

Outcomes are restricted to those that are neither very rare nor near-universal among untreated villages near the threshold (a symmetric prevalence band), justified by concern about underpowered tests and type M error for rare outcomes.
observations.quote: type M error in cases of a statistically significant estimate

observations.statement: Villages are matched to GPs via the 2021 Local Government Directory for the post-2015 period and a Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation panel matched by population and fuzzy name matching for 1995-2014; match rates are reported for both linkages and are high.
observations.locator: Section II, Matching Villages to GPs

observations.statement: Every regression table reports the effective number of observations and the estimation bandwidth for each column, both varying by outcome because of outcome-specific bandwidth selection.

Multi-outcome indices for education, infrastructure, workfare and programs are built following Kling, Liebman, and Katz (2007) as equally weighted averages of z-scores relative to the mean and SD among villages just below the cutoff, addressing multiple hypothesis testing.

Treatment is a dummy for village population at or above the cutoff (one thousand) in the relevant pre-delimitation census, with the running variable being that same census population recentered at the cutoff.
Candidate wealth (movable and immovable assets) is transformed with the inverse hyperbolic sine because of substantial dispersion and many zero values in the election affidavit data.
For the alternative RD, the running variable is redefined as the population of other villages in the same pre-2015 GP after dropping the village whose population is closest to the cutoff.
observations.locator: Section III / Section IV.D alternative RD construction

observations.statement: Authors note census village boundaries remain essentially fixed over the panel, with splits rare and concentrated among small villages far from the discontinuity, arguing this does not threaten identification.

Each results table reports the RD point estimate, clustered standard error, bracketed p-value, dependent-variable mean among below-cutoff villages, bandwidth, and effective observations for every column.
Table notes uniformly restate that standard errors are clustered at the gram panchayat level and that reported brackets contain p-values rather than significance stars.
All main specifications state use of a triangular kernel with MSE-optimal bandwidth selection following Calonico et al. (2017), repeated as the default estimating convention in every table note.

Table 4 augments the baseline RD specification with a continuous interaction term between the treatment dummy and rescaled prior GP population, reported alongside the unadjusted RD estimate in the same columns.
Standard errors are clustered at the gram panchayat level throughout, which the authors align with the level at which GP-assignment treatment is determined.
For the election-outcome table, the Romano-Wolf correction is applied to control the family-wise error rate across the multiple outcomes tested in that table.
Confidence intervals for the average of main versus placebo RD coefficients in Figure 4 are built by block bootstrapping at the pre-2015 GP level over 500 replications.

A manipulation/density test (Cattaneo, Jansson, and Ma 2018) is reported in the main text for the two census population distributions used as running variables, with the p-values stated in the text; the corresponding plot sits in the online appendix.

Table 1 tests six pre-delimitation covariates, including school presence, paved road, electrification, scheduled-caste share and literacy, for discontinuities at the population cutoff, and reports the estimate for each covariate in its own row.
Table 1 column 1 and Figure 1 report the first-stage effect of crossing the village population cutoff on the resulting GP's population, separately for the 1995 and 2015 delimitations.

Robustness to a CER-optimal bandwidth, fixed bandwidths of 100 and 200, a quadratic polynomial, and a uniform kernel is summarized in the main text with the underlying tables placed in the online appendix.
observations.locator: Section IV.E, Robustness to Other RD Specifications

observations.statement: Figure 4 summarizes sixteen placebo estimates from four placebo strategies (other states, noncompliant UP districts, the earlier-census cutoff, split-ineligible villages) against the real RD estimates in one coefficient plot and discusses how many placebos reach conventional significance.
Match rates between administrative datasets and the census backbone are reported and tested for discontinuity at the population cutoff, and found unrelated to treatment status.

A robustness check drops villages potentially contaminated by simultaneous nearby splits near the 2015 threshold; the main text reports the comparison with the baseline programs-index estimate in one sentence and places the full results in the online appendix.

A spillover check tests whether blocks with a higher share of just-above-cutoff villages show worse outcomes in nearby just-below-cutoff villages within the same block; no evidence of negative spillovers is found, with details in the online appendix.

A financing robustness check uses GP accounting data to test whether smaller GPs mechanically receive more per-capita funding or benefit from fixed-allocation formulas, with details in the online appendix.

Table 6 splits the sample four ways (largest pre-delimitation village, pradhan's home village, direction of caste-fractionalization change, single versus multi-habitation) and reports separate RD estimates with equality-of-coefficients p-values for each split.
Table 4 estimates heterogeneity continuously by interacting the RD treatment indicator with rescaled prior GP population rather than relying only on discrete population bins.
Authors explicitly flag that subsample-by-population-bin heterogeneity results are underpowered and that apparent nonlinearities across counterfactual polity sizes cannot be established definitively.
observations.quote: we lack statistical power to say this definitively

observations.statement: The five main outcome families are each first summarized as a single index effect measured in standard-deviation units before decomposing into component outcomes.

Component-outcome coefficients are routinely translated into a percent-of-mean change alongside the raw coefficient, for example a percentage-point increase in toilet ownership relative to its below-cutoff mean.

The magnitude of the gram-sabha-attendance increase is interpreted with reference to Das (2015), who links a similarly sized attendance change to sizable SD increases in sanitation and health facility provision.

The conclusion reports a back-of-envelope cost-benefit figure, a direct annual cost per resident of creating a polity, drawn from a detailed online appendix analysis and weighed against estimated service-delivery benefits.

Authors acknowledge that crossing the threshold bundles multiple simultaneous changes in population, geographic compactness and homogeneity, complicating isolation of which component drives the estimated effects.

Authors state that statistical power, particularly for the individually targeted programs outcome, limits how strongly they can characterize nonlinearities in treatment effects across counterfactual polity sizes.

Authors note they cannot separate whether infrastructure improvements reflect greater leader lobbying effort or reduced corruption, since outcome measures capture on-the-ground presence rather than either channel individually.
observations.quote: even if we cannot disentangle the two

observations.statement: Mechanism evidence in Section V is repeatedly described as more suggestive than definitive, since a village's political weight or other characteristics could correlate with unobserved sources of heterogeneity.
Figures 1 through 3 present binned-scatter RD plots, showing population bins with fitted polynomial lines, for the first stage, main outcome indices, and heterogeneity coefficients.
Tables report exact p-values in brackets below clustered standard errors rather than significance stars, with every table note restating the clustering level and RD estimation convention.
Heterogeneity-by-population-bin results and the robustness/placebo summary are both presented as coefficient plots with confidence intervals rather than solely as regression tables.
Online appendix tables and figures are consistently labeled with an A prefix, for example Table A3 or Figure A10, and are cross-referenced by number throughout the main text.
The introduction previews the paper's main quantitative findings in detail, including education, housing, sanitation, workfare and targeting results, before the empirical strategy is described.
A roadmap paragraph at the end of the introduction states the section-by-section organization of the paper.
observations.quote: Section I discusses the institutional background

observations.statement: The introduction contains explicit contribution paragraphs positioning the paper against three literatures: causal estimates of polity size, decentralization theory, and local-government design for public goods provision.
Robustness checks are consolidated into their own labeled subsection at the end of the results section rather than interspersed with each individual result.
Mechanism analysis occupies its own section after all main results, organized around four theory-linked channels, and relies heavily on online appendix material for supporting detail throughout.
Subsample splits by prior largest-village status and pradhan home village in Table 6 are used to distinguish an electoral-incentive mechanism from a locally based leadership mechanism.
Civic engagement measures and candidate characteristics such as criminal record, caste and wealth are used as intermediate outcomes to test political-behavior and political-selection channels.
Elite capture, geographic compactness, and caste homogeneity are each tested using heterogeneity splits and explicitly ruled out as drivers of the main results.

The main RD estimates are explicitly characterized as a local average treatment effect of moving into a GP of about the cutoff size (one thousand residents) from a range of counterfactual populations, not a population-average decentralization effect.

Authors state findings are most directly applicable to north Indian local government design but argue the political mechanisms plausibly generalize to other democratic states with similar local government structures.
A data-and-code citation with an ICPSR DOI is listed in the references, indicating a public openICPSR replication package associated with the paper.

The rdrobust Stata command and its methodological references (Calonico, Cattaneo, and Titiunik 2014; Calonico et al. 2017) are explicitly named as the estimation software used throughout the empirical strategy.

Most outcome and covariate data derive from government administrative sources such as the Census of India, SECC, Mission Antyodaya, the NREGS portal, and the State Election Commission rather than original survey collection.

concordance.paper_says: Local polynomial (linear) sharp RD estimated via rdrobust (Calonico, Cattaneo, and Titiunik 2014; Calonico et al. 2017), triangular kernel, MSE-optimal bandwidth (Section III).
concordance.card_shows: specifications s1-s5 all record estimator=local_linear_rd, command=rdrobust.

concordance.paper_says: Equation (1) is a cross-sectional RD with polynomial controls only; no fixed effects are described (Section III).
concordance.card_shows: fixed_effects is null for specifications s1-s5.

concordance.paper_says: Standard errors clustered at the gram panchayat level throughout (footnote 11 and all table notes).
concordance.card_shows: se.type=cluster for s1-s5; cluster_level resolved to gp_code_jj11_num or gp_code_lgd21_num for s2-s5, unresolved (null) for s1.

concordance.paper_says: Heterogeneity-robust standard errors clustered at the GP level are used for all reported estimates (footnote 11).
concordance.card_shows: se.type recorded as cluster for every specification (s1-s5).

concordance.paper_says: MSE-optimal bandwidth (Calonico, Cattaneo, and Titiunik 2014; Calonico et al. 2017) is the default, varying by outcome; robustness uses CER-optimal and fixed bandwidths of 100 and 200 (Section IV.E, online appendix).
concordance.card_shows: diagnostic x2 records bandwidth_selection status=observed, MSE-optimal bandwidth computed via rdbwselect inside the MultiPanelTabRD wrapper.

concordance.paper_says: Villages just below the 1,000-population cutoff serve as the comparison group for villages just above (Section III).
concordance.card_shows: comparison_group is null in design d1 and in all specifications s1-s5.

concordance.paper_says: As one of several checks that another program does not use the same threshold, the paper reruns the main outcome in the subset of noncompliant districts (Section III, Section IV.E).
concordance.card_shows: s4.sample = noncompliant_district_1995==0 and s5.sample = noncompliant_district_1995==1, role=robustness.

concordance.paper_says: A density/manipulation test (Cattaneo, Jansson, and Ma 2018) is reported in the main text with p=0.44 (1991) and p=0.35 (2011) (Section III).
concordance.card_shows: diagnostic x1 (density_test) has status=not_found_in_scope; rddensity is installed but its usage was not traced within the files the card read.

concordance.paper_says: A linear polynomial (p=1) is used in all main and robustness specifications (Section III, table notes).
concordance.card_shows: diagnostic x3 (polynomial_order) status=observed, p=1 default in MultiPanelTabRD, verified in table notes.

concordance.paper_says: Section IV.E and the online appendix describe alternative bandwidths, a quadratic polynomial, a uniform kernel, spillover tests, financing/funding-formula tests, and dropping potentially contaminated villages (Section IV.E).
concordance.card_shows: the card's top-level robustness array is empty; these checks are not captured as discrete items.

concordance.paper_says: Six numbered tables (Table 1 first stage/balance, Table 2 village amenities, Table 3 service delivery, Table 4 heterogeneity by population size, Table 5 election outcomes, Table 6 heterogeneity by past GP composition) plus four figures.
concordance.card_shows: outputs.tables lists t1-t5 with captions matching Tables 1, 2, 3, and 5 and a file path for a table labeled table4.tex; outputs.figures is empty.

concordance.paper_says: Village-level analysis datasets cover amenities, village directory, finances, NREGS, Mission Antyodaya, GP elections and GP development plans (Section II).
concordance.card_shows: data[] lists amenities_analysis.dta and village_analysis_cleaned.dta (unit=village); conventions[] separately notes analysis_data subfolders for financial, nregs, mission_antyodaya, gp_elections, gp_development_plan.

gaps: No explicit discussion of a few-clusters problem or wild-bootstrap inference, despite some robustness specifications clustering on relatively few GP-level clusters.
No pre-analysis plan, IRB approval, or ethics statement is mentioned anywhere in the main text (preregistration_or_ethics category not observed).
No standalone descriptive summary-statistics table appears in the main text; dependent-variable means are reported only inside each results table.

Recipe card diagnostic x1 (density test) is marked not_found_in_scope even though the paper reports specific density-test p-values in the main text; the implementing code was outside the card's partial read scope.
The paper's placebo and robustness checks (Section IV.E, online appendices C-F) are not captured as discrete items in the recipe card, whose top-level robustness array is empty.

The Online Appendix (Appendices A-J), referenced dozens of times for supplementary figures, tables and detailed derivations, is a separate document not included in the provided source text and could not be read.

reading.note: Read all 43 pages of the extracted text in full: title/abstract, introduction, institutional background, data, empirical strategy, all results subsections (IV.A-E), mechanisms (V.A-D), conclusion, and the reference list; page 43 of the raw form-feed split is a blank trailing artifact with no content. The paper's Online Appendix, cited extensively throughout for additional figures, tables and robustness detail, is a separate document not included in this source text and was not read; observations describing appendix content rely on the main text's own description of what the appendix contains. Numeric results scrubbed from statements on 2026-09-08 (paper-practice-v1 rule: no numerical results).
